title: Subscriptions & Bills
description: Tame the charges that come back every month.
wolfLine: Every subscription is a little hand in your pocket. Count the hands.

subscription.definition: A service that charges you again and again, monthly or yearly, until you cancel.
subscription.example: A $15.99 streaming service billed on the 4th of every month.

auto-renewal.definition: When a subscription renews and charges you automatically unless you cancel first.
auto-renewal.example: Your yearly app plan charges $59.99 again on its anniversary.

free-trial.definition: A free taste of a paid service that usually turns into a paid subscription when it ends, unless you cancel.
free-trial.example: Seven days free, then $14.99 a month on the card you entered.

utility.definition: A basic home service you pay for as you use it, like electricity, water, gas or trash.
utility.example: A water bill based on how many gallons you used.

autopay.definition: Letting a company take a bill out of your account automatically each month.
autopay.example: Your phone bill pulls itself from checking on the 14th.

promotional-rate.definition: A low starting price for new customers that jumps after a set time, often 12 months.
promotional-rate.example: Internet at $40 a month for year one, then $70.

lessons.title: The Subscription Pile
lessons.summary: Little monthly charges, big yearly totals.

steps.context: A [[subscription]] charges you again and again, monthly or yearly, until you cancel.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a subscription?
choices: A streaming service that bills you every month
steps.explain: It charges again every month until you stop it.

steps.prompt: You pay for 4 streaming services: $12, $16, $9 and $15 a month. What’s the monthly total?
What’s that over a year?
Small subscriptions are harmless because each one is cheap.
steps.explain: Five $10 subscriptions are $600 a year.

steps.context: Most subscriptions have [[auto-renewal]]: they renew and charge you automatically unless you cancel first.
steps.prompt: Your yearly app plan renews tomorrow and you never use it. What do you do?
why: That’s another year paid for something you don’t use.
Deleting the app doesn’t cancel the subscription. You’d keep paying.
steps.explain: Cancel before the renewal date and you won’t be charged again.

steps.prompt: A subscription keeps charging you until you ___.
steps.explain: Only canceling stops the charges.

lessons.title: Free Trials
lessons.summary: Free until it isn’t. Set the reminder.

steps.context: A [[free trial]] gives you a service free for a while, but you usually enter your card first. When it ends, it becomes a paid subscription.
steps.prompt: Why do free trials ask for your card?
choices: So they can start charging when the trial ends
steps.explain: The card is how “free” becomes “paid.”

steps.prompt: Best habit when you start a free trial?
choices: Set a reminder to cancel a day or two before it ends
Use a different email each time
steps.explain: Reminders beat memory every time.

steps.prompt: You forget to cancel a trial for a $14.99-a-month app and notice 3 months later. How much did you pay?
Canceling a free trial early usually still lets you use it until the trial ends.
steps.explain: Most services keep it running to the end date, so cancel right after signing up.

steps.prompt: You only meant to try FitPro for free. Tap the charge to stop.
steps.explain: The trial ended and turned into a paid plan.

steps.prompt: A “free” gift box only asks you to pay $4.95 shipping. What should you check first?
choices: Whether it signs you up for a monthly subscription
steps.explain: “Just pay shipping” offers often hide a monthly plan in the small print.

lessons.title: Subscription Audit
lessons.summary: List every repeating charge. Keep what earns its place.

steps.title: Once a year, audit everything
steps.body: Pull up your last two months of statements and list every repeating charge. For each one, ask: did I use this in the last month? Would I sign up again today, at this price?

steps.prompt: You haven’t been to the gym since spring. Tap the subscription to cancel first.
steps.explain: The biggest charge, for something you don’t use.

steps.prompt: Add up every subscription on this statement.
How much does canceling the gym save over a year?
Keep or cancel?
items: Music app you use every day
Gym you haven’t visited in 4 months
A second streaming service you forgot about

steps.prompt: Not sure whether you’ll miss it?
choices: Cancel it. You can always sign up again
Pay for a full year upfront
steps.explain: If you miss it, rejoin. Most people never do.

lessons.title: Utility Bills
lessons.summary: Read a water bill and see which part you control.

steps.context: A [[utility]] is a basic home service you pay for as you use it: electricity, water, gas, trash.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a utility?
steps.explain: A basic home service you pay for as you use it.

steps.prompt: A bill says “Estimated reading.” What does that mean?
choices: They guessed your usage, and the next real reading will correct it
You don’t have to pay it
steps.explain: Pay it, but expect an adjustment next time.

lessons.title: Autopay: Friend or Foe
lessons.summary: Never miss a due date, without getting blindsided.

steps.context: [[Autopay]] lets a company take the bill out of your account automatically every month.
steps.prompt: What’s the biggest upside of autopay?
choices: You never miss a due date
You never need to look at them again
steps.explain: No late fees from forgetting.

steps.prompt: What’s the biggest risk?
choices: A bill pulls when your account is low and overdraws it
steps.explain: Autopay doesn’t check your balance first.

steps.prompt: With autopay on, you can stop reading your bills.
steps.explain: A wrong charge on autopay just gets paid. Still read every bill.

steps.prompt: Good fit for autopay?
items: Rent that’s the same every month
A phone plan with a fixed price
Electricity that swings with the seasons
A bill you think has mistakes

steps.prompt: Payday is the 15th. Your phone autopay pulls on the 10th, when your account is lowest. What’s the fix?
choices: Move the autopay date to after the 15th
steps.explain: Most companies let you choose the date. Line it up with payday.

steps.prompt: Your account has $310. Three autopays hit on the same day: $85 phone, $140 insurance, $95 internet. How much are you short?

lessons.title: Your Bill Calendar
lessons.summary: Line up due dates with paydays so no week is a surprise.

steps.title: Every bill, on one page
steps.body: Write down every bill, its amount and its due date, then sort them by date. Now you can see which paycheck pays what, and which week is tight.

steps.prompt: Put these bills in due-date order.
steps.explain: Earliest first.

steps.prompt: Bills due between the 1st and the 14th: rent $1,100, internet $60, phone $45. How much has to come from your first paycheck?
Your first paycheck is $1,250. How much is left after those bills?
That leaves $45 for two weeks of food. What helps?
choices: Ask to move a due date later in the month
steps.explain: Moving the phone bill to the 20th puts it on the second paycheck.

steps.prompt: Many companies will move your due date if you ask.
steps.explain: It’s usually a two-minute call or a setting in your account.

steps.context: A [[promotional rate]] is a low price for new customers that jumps after a set time, often 12 months.
steps.prompt: Your internet was $40 a month for the first year and is now $70. What happened?
steps.explain: Introductory prices quietly expire.

steps.prompt: How much more is that per year?
What’s the best first move?
choices: Call and ask for a better rate, mentioning other offers
steps.explain: Companies often have a retention offer for customers who ask.

steps.prompt: Over one year, which is cheaper?
How much does switching save in the first year?
Phone, internet and insurance prices are often negotiable.
steps.explain: Ask once a year. The worst they can say is no.

lessons.title: Monthly or Yearly?
lessons.summary: Paying upfront saves money, if you’ll really use it.

steps.context: Many subscriptions are cheaper if you pay for a whole year at once.
steps.prompt: $12 a month, or $99 for the year. Which is cheaper over a full year?
steps.explain: Monthly: $12 × 12 = $144. Yearly: $99.

steps.prompt: How much does the yearly plan save?
When is the yearly plan a bad idea?
choices: When you’re not sure you’ll use it all year
steps.explain: A discount on something you stop using isn’t a saving.

steps.prompt: You’d quit after 6 months. What would monthly cost you?
So for 6 months of use, which was cheaper?
steps.explain: $72 beats $99 if you only use it half the year.

steps.prompt: A yearly plan auto-renews too, so set a reminder before it does.
steps.explain: Otherwise next year’s $99 arrives on its own.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Subscriptions & Bills
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Three subscriptions at $11, $15 and $8 a month. What do they cost in a year?
Deleting an app cancels its subscription.
steps.explain: You have to cancel the subscription itself.

steps.prompt: Internet was $45 for a year and is now $75. What ended?
steps.explain: The intro price expired.

steps.prompt: What’s the main risk of autopay?
choices: It can overdraw your account if the balance is low
steps.explain: Line autopay dates up with payday.
